theme: The corruption of creation; Noah finds grace; the ark commanded
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 6:1-22 slowly. This is one of the most sobering chapters in the Bible. It contains both the grimmest assessment of human depravity in the Old Testament and the first glimpse of God’s grace toward a particular man. As you read, notice the contrast between verses 5 and 8.
settingTheScene:
Yesterday we walked through ten generations from Adam to Noah, watching death claim each generation in turn while the line of promise quietly continued. Today we arrive at the crisis point. Sin has not just spread, it has saturated. The world God called “very good” in Genesis 1 has become a world God grieves over in Genesis 6. The chapter we read today is the prelude to the flood. It is also the chapter where the word “grace” first appears in the Bible.

The chapter has several unusual features that have puzzled interpreters for centuries, the sons of God taking the daughters of men, the Nephilim, the lifespan limit of 120 years. These are real interpretive challenges, but they are not the point of the chapter. The point is this: humanity has become so corrupt that God will start over, but one man has found grace.
observation: The chapter opens with a strange episode (verses 1-4) about the “sons of God” taking the “daughters of man” as wives. Many interpretations exist; the text itself is sparse.
Verse 3: “My Spirit shall not abide in man forever, for he is flesh: his days shall be 120 years.” This may be a divine deadline before the flood, or a general statement on human lifespan.
Verse 5 is one of the bleakest assessments of humanity in the Bible: “every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”
Verse 6 attributes genuine emotion to God: he was “grieved” and his heart “was sorrowful.” God is not impassive in the face of human sin.
Verse 8 is the hinge of the chapter: “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.” The Hebrew word for “favor” here is hen, the first appearance of the word grace in Scripture.
Noah is described as “a righteous man, blameless in his generation. Noah walked with God.” The same phrase used of Enoch.
The ark’s dimensions are precise: 300 cubits long, 50 wide, 30 high. Roughly 450 feet by 75 feet by 45 feet.
God establishes a “covenant” with Noah (verse 18) before the flood comes, the first explicit use of the word covenant in the Bible.
The chapter ends: “Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.” Obedience born of grace.
interpretation:
Genesis 6 is one of the most theologically loaded chapters in the entire Bible. In just twenty-two verses, we see the depth of human sin, the genuine sorrow of God, the first mention of grace, the introduction of the word covenant, and the obedience of one man who walks with God against the entire grain of his culture.

The chapter opens with a mysterious passage (verses 1-4) about the “sons of God” who take the “daughters of man” as wives, producing offspring described as Nephilim and “mighty men of old, men of renown.” Three main interpretations have been offered through church history: that the sons of God were fallen angels, that they were powerful human rulers, or that they were descendants of the godly line of Seth intermarrying with the corrupt line of Cain. The text itself is sparse, and good Christian interpreters have differed. What matters for our purposes is the result: a further escalation of human corruption that prompts God’s verdict in verse 3 and his action in verses 5-7.

Verse 5 is the most devastating sentence in the Old Testament about the human condition. “The LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” Every intention. Of the thoughts. Of the heart. Only evil. Continually. This is total depravity in narrative form. The doctrine of sin you read about on Day 6 is not a theological abstraction; it is what God himself saw when he looked at his creation a few generations after Adam.

And then comes one of the most surprising verses in the Old Testament. Verse 6: “And the LORD was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart.” This is not the cool, detached God of philosophy. This is a God who genuinely feels. He grieves over what humanity has become. He is sorrowful over the broken relationship with his image-bearers. We must be careful not to read this as a God who was surprised, the same Bible insists that God knows the end from the beginning. But we must also not flatten this into a metaphor. The God of the Bible has real affections, and human sin really grieves him.

Then verse 8, in the middle of the catastrophe: “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.” The conjunction is everything. The world is drowning in evil, and God is grieving, BUT Noah found grace. The Hebrew word translated “favor” is hen, which appears here for the first time in Scripture and will run through the entire Old Testament as the language of unmerited divine kindness. Notice carefully what the text does not say. It does not say Noah earned God’s favor or deserved God’s favor. It says he found it. Grace, by definition, is found, not earned. And then it tells us what kind of man Noah was: righteous, blameless in his generation, walking with God. This is not the basis of his grace; it is the fruit of it. Noah’s righteousness is what grace had made of him in a world where everyone else was evil.

The rest of the chapter is the introduction of a new covenant arrangement. God reveals his judgment plan to Noah, gives him precise instructions for the ark, and says: “I will establish my covenant with you” (verse 18). This is the first use of the word “covenant” (berith) in the Bible. From this point on, covenant will be the central category of biblical theology. God always relates to his people through covenant, first with Noah, then with Abraham, then with Israel at Sinai, then with David, and finally through the new covenant in Christ. Genesis 6 is where this great covenantal story begins.

The chapter ends with a single, climactic sentence: “Noah did this; he did all that God commanded him.” It would have taken many decades to build the ark. The world was watching, probably mocking. There was no rain yet, Noah was building a sea-going vessel inland, on God’s word alone. And he did everything God commanded. This is what faith looks like when grace meets a person: obedience that does not need to see results before it acts.
connection: Yesterday’s genealogy showed the line of promise being preserved through Seth and his descendants. Genesis 6 narrows the focus to one man, Noah. The doctrine of sin you encountered on Day 6 is here demonstrated in its most extreme form: every intention of the human heart was only evil continually. And the doctrine of grace, which the rest of the Bible will develop, makes its first explicit appearance: “Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.” From the very beginning of Scripture, the pattern is set, humanity in rebellion, God in patient grief, and one chosen by grace to receive what others cannot. This pattern will repeat with Abraham, with Israel, and ultimately in Christ, who alone is the truly righteous one through whom all who are in him are preserved through the judgment to come.
application:
Sit with verse 5 for a moment before you move on. “Every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” This is what God saw when he looked at humanity then, and it is what God still sees when he looks at humanity now apart from his grace. Not just bad behavior on the surface, but evil running all the way down to the intentions of the heart. This is not exaggeration. It is what your Maker sees.

And sit with verse 8. “But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.” Grace is the only difference between you and the world headed for judgment. Not your morality, your church attendance, your good intentions, your spiritual disciplines, your theology. Grace. God’s free, unearned, unmerited choice to set his favor on you in Christ.

Today, consider three things. First, take your own sin seriously. The same evil that filled the earth in Noah’s day is still in human hearts, yours included. Do not minimize what God grieves over. Second, take grace seriously. You did not find God; he found you. Whatever righteousness has been worked in your life is the fruit of grace, not its cause. Be humble about it. Third, take obedience seriously. Noah heard God’s word and obeyed in a world that thought he was crazy. If you are following Christ today in ways that confuse or anger people around you, you are in good company. Build your ark. The flood is real. And Christ is the door.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you see in your own heart when you look honestly at it.
Thank him for the grace that has found you apart from any merit of your own.
Ask him for the kind of obedience Noah showed, even when it looks foolish to others.
